title: India's Bid to Become a Global Education Hub Faces a Reality Check
excerpt: Despite ambitious targets under the National Education Policy 2020, India hosts just 72,000 foreign students — a fraction of what rivals attract — and the gap between policy rhetoric and campus reality remains wide.
body:
• India hosted approximately 72,218 foreign students in 2025, a modest recovery from the pandemic-era low of 48,000 but far below its target of 200,000 by 2030
  • For every 22 Indian students studying abroad, the country attracts only one international student, highlighting a severe imbalance in educational mobility
  • The government has set a long-term goal of hosting 500,000 foreign students by 2047, but gaps in infrastructure, visa processing, and post-study employment persist
  • India lacks post-study employment pathways for international graduates, unlike competitors such as the US, UK, Canada, and Australia

The Paradox of Policy and Performance

India's ambition to position itself as a global education hub is running into an uncomfortable paradox: even as policy pushes intensify under the National Education Policy 2020, international student inflows remain modest and have shown signs of stagnation. After peaking at nearly 75,000 international students in 2019, enrollments fell sharply during the pandemic and recovered only partially, suggesting that India has struggled to rebuild momentum.

The numbers tell a stark story. India hosted approximately 72,218 foreign students from about 200 countries in 2025, according to government data. While that represents an improvement from the 48,000 recorded in 2021, the base remains small compared to other major destinations. The United States hosts more than a million international students annually, the United Kingdom nearly 700,000, and even smaller systems like Australia attract well over 500,000.

"India's share of globally mobile students remains negligible. For every 22 Indian students studying abroad, the country attracts only one international student."

— Diya Dutt, Adviser, Association of Indian Universities

Ambition Outpaces Infrastructure

The government has set a target of attracting 200,000 foreign students annually by 2030 — a fourfold increase from current levels — under the 'Study in India' initiative. Longer term, it aims to host 500,000 foreign students by 2047. Both targets demand a level of investment in campus infrastructure, student support services, and regulatory reform that India has not yet demonstrated at scale.

Reforms under NEP 2020 have produced some visible changes. More than 800 Indian higher education institutions have registered with the Study in India program, which offers tuition waivers and a centralized admissions process. Institutions can now reserve up to 25% supernumerary seats for international students, and regulations have been introduced to allow foreign university campuses to operate in India.

But the gap between announcement and execution remains wide. "Students face obstacles in terms of visas and residence permit process which sours their study experience," said Diya Dutt, an adviser at the Association of Indian Universities. IIM Kozhikode reported a 42% increase in international applications over the past year, but the absolute numbers remain small, and a majority of applicants continue to come from Nepal.

The Missing Post-Study Pathway

Perhaps the most significant structural disadvantage India faces in the global competition for students is the absence of post-study employment opportunities for international graduates. Unlike the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia — all of which offer formal work authorization pathways after graduation — India currently provides no such mechanism.

"Foreign students not only seek quality education but pathways for employment after completing their studies. India currently does not offer post-study employment opportunities for international students," Dutt said. The Niti Aayog, India's policy think tank, has recommended at minimum allowing international students to complete internships during or after their programs, but the recommendation has not been implemented.

Quality perceptions also pose a challenge. While India was the highest-represented country in the Times Higher Education Impact Rankings 2025 with 147 institutions, many universities — particularly lower-ranked ones — are still building research capacity and international visibility. "Strengthening research output and global engagement is essential to improve institutional reputation," Dutt said.

A report by Deloitte India and Knight Frank India estimated that by hosting more foreign university campuses and retaining a larger share of students domestically, India could save $113 billion in foreign currency outflows by 2040. Three foreign universities have already opened campuses in India, with more expected within the next two years, though skeptics question whether satellite campuses can replicate the experience of studying abroad.
